facts.statement: The hoopoe starling lived on the island of Réunion and went extinct around 1850.
facts.quote: The hoopoe starling (Fregilupus varius), also known as the Réunion starling or the Bourbon crested starling, is a species of starling that lived on the Mascarene island of Réunion and became extinct in the 1850s.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling measured 30 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The hoopoe starling was 30 cm in length.

facts.statement: The bird had white and grey plumage with darker brown and grey on its back, wings, and tail.
facts.quote: Its plumage was primarily white and grey, with its back, wings and tail a darker brown and grey.

facts.statement: The species possessed a light, mobile crest that curled forward.
facts.quote: It had a light, mobile crest, which curled forwards.

facts.statement: Males were likely larger than females and had more curved beaks.
facts.quote: The bird is thought to have been sexually dimorphic, with males larger and having more curved beaks.

facts.statement: The bird likely lived in large flocks within humid areas and marshes.
facts.quote: Reportedly living in large flocks, it inhabited humid areas and marshes.

facts.statement: It was an omnivore that fed on plant matter and insects.
facts.quote: The hoopoe starling was omnivorous, feeding on plant matter and insects.

facts.statement: Its robust pelvis, large feet and claws, and strong jaws suggest it foraged near the ground.
facts.quote: Its pelvis was robust, its feet and claws large, and its jaws strong, indicating that it foraged near the ground.

facts.statement: The bird was first mentioned in the 17th century and was long believed to be related to the hoopoe.
facts.quote: The bird was first mentioned during the 17th century and was long thought to be related to the hoopoe, from which its name is derived.

facts.statement: Settlers on Réunion hunted the birds for food and kept them as pets.
facts.quote: The birds were hunted by settlers on Réunion, who also kept them as pets.

facts.statement: Nineteen museum specimens of the species exist worldwide.
facts.quote: Nineteen specimens exist in museums around the world.

facts.statement: The earliest potential mention of the bird is a 1658 list by French governor Étienne de Flacourt.
facts.quote: The first account thought to mention the hoopoe starling is a 1658 list of birds of Madagascar written by French governor Étienne de Flacourt.

facts.statement: Père Vachet first noted the bird on Réunion in 1669, and Sieur Dubois described it in detail in 1674.
facts.quote: The hoopoe starling was first noted on the Mascarene island of Réunion (then called "Bourbon") by Père Vachet in 1669, and first described in detail by French traveler Sieur Dubois's in 1674

facts.statement: The species was first scientifically described by Philippe Guéneau de Montbeillard in 1779, with the name finalized by Pieter Boddaert in 1783.
facts.quote: The species was first scientifically described by French naturalist Philippe Guéneau de Montbeillard in the 1779 edition of French naturalist Comte de Buffon's Histoire Naturelle, and received its scientific name from Dutch naturalist Pieter Boddaert for the book's 1783 edition.

facts.statement: Hermann Schlegel proposed in 1857 that the bird belonged to the starling family, reclassifying it as Sturnus capensis.
facts.quote: German ornithologist Hermann Schlegel first proposed in 1857 that the species belonged to the starling family, (Sturnidae), reclassifying it as part of the genus Sturnus, S. capensis.

facts.statement: Carl Jakob Sundevall proposed the genus Lophopsarus in 1872, but Fregilupus varius remains the valid binomial name.
facts.quote: Swedish zoologist Carl Jakob Sundevall proposed the new genus name Lophopsarus ("crested starling") in 1872, yet Fregilupus varius—the oldest name—remains the bird's binomial, and all other scientific names are synonyms.

facts.statement: James Murie confirmed in 1874 that the bird was a starling based on the analysis of its skeleton.
facts.quote: In 1874, after a detailed analysis of the only known skeleton (held at the Cambridge University Museum of Zoology), British zoologist James Murie agreed that it was a starling.

facts.statement: Andrew John Berger cast doubt on the bird's relationship with starlings in 1957 due to subtle anatomical differences.
facts.quote: In 1957, American ornithologist Andrew John Berger cast doubt on the bird's affinity with starlings because of subtle anatomical differences, after dissecting a spirit specimen at the American Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: A relationship with vangas was proposed by some authors but rejected by Hiroyuki Morioka in 1996.
facts.quote: Some authors proposed a relationship with vangas (Vangidae), but Japanese ornithologist Hiroyuki Morioka rejected this in 1996, after a comparative study of skulls.

facts.statement: Subfossil bones found on Rodrigues led to the description of the Rodrigues starling in 1879.
facts.quote: In 1879, these bones became the basis for a new species, Necropsar rodericanus (the Rodrigues starling), named by British ornithologists Albert Günther and Edward Newton.

facts.statement: Subfossils found in 1974 confirmed the Rodrigues starling is a distinct genus from Fregilupus due to its stouter bill.
facts.quote: Subfossils found in 1974 confirmed that the Rodrigues bird was a distinct genus of starling; primarily, its stouter bill warrants generic separation from Fregilupus.

facts.statement: Julian P. Hume described the Mauritius starling in 2014, noting it is closer to the Rodrigues starling than the hoopoe starling.
facts.quote: In 2014, British palaeontologist Julian P. Hume described a new extinct species, the Mauritius starling (Cryptopsar ischyrhynchus), based on subfossils from Mauritius, which was closer to the Rodrigues starling than to the hoopoe starling in its skull, sternal (breastbone), and humeral features.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling measured 30 cm in length.
facts.quote: The hoopoe starling was 30 cm in length.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling was the largest of the three Mascarene starlings.
facts.quote: It was the largest of the three Mascarene starlings.

facts.statement: A presumed adult male specimen in the Paris museum had a light ash-grey head and neck with a long crest of the same color featuring white shafts.
facts.quote: A presumed adult male (NHMUK 1889.5.30.15) in the Paris museum has a light ash-grey head and back of the neck (lighter on the hind-neck), with a long crest the same colour with white shafts.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling had ash-brown back and tail, darker wings with a greyish wash, and upper tail coverts and rump with a rufous wash.
facts.quote: Its back and tail are ash-brown, its wings darker with a greyish wash, and its upper tail covert feathers and rump have a rufous wash.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling had lemon-yellow beaks and legs with yellow-brown claws.
facts.quote: The beak and legs are lemon-yellow, with yellow-brown claws.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling had a bare, triangular patch of skin around the eye that may have been yellow in life.
facts.quote: It has a bare, triangular area of skin around the eye, which may have been yellow in life.

facts.statement: An observer named Vinson described the hoopoe starling's crest as flexible, composed of disunited forward-curled barbs of varying lengths, highest in the center, and capable of being erected at will.
facts.quote: Vinson, who observed live hoopoe starlings when he lived on Réunion, described the crest as flexible, disunited and forward-curled barbs of various lengths, highest in the centre, and able to be erected at will.

facts.statement: The only illustration of the hoopoe starling believed to be drawn from life was created by French artist Paul Philippe Sauguin de Jossigny in the early 1770s.
facts.quote: The only illustration of the hoopoe starling now thought to have been made from life was drawn by French artist Paul Philippe Sauguin de Jossigny during the early 1770s.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling had a narrow, strongly decurved upper beak and a narrow, sharply pointed lower beak.
facts.quote: The upper beak was narrow and strongly decurved, and the lower beak was narrow and sharply pointed.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling possessed an extremely robust pelvis.
facts.quote: The pelvis was extremely robust.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling's femur was robust, particularly at the upper and lower ends, with a straight shaft.
facts.quote: The femur (thigh bone) was robust, especially at the upper and lower ends, and the shaft was straight.

facts.statement: In 1943, American ornithologist Dean Amadon suggested that Sturnus-like species arrived in Africa and gave rise to the wattled starling and Mascarene starlings.
facts.quote: In 1943, American ornithologist Dean Amadon suggested that Sturnus-like species could have arrived in Africa and given rise to the wattled starling (Creatophora cinerea) and the Mascarene starlings.

facts.statement: In 2008, Dario Zuccon and colleagues used a toe-pad sample from a Stockholm specimen to confirm the hoopoe starling's status as an isolated lineage of Southeast Asian starlings.
facts.quote: A 2008 study by Italian zoologist Dario Zuccon and colleagues analysing the DNA of a variety of starlings confirmed that the hoopoe starling belonged in a clade of Southeast Asian starlings as an isolated lineage, with no close relatives. They used a toe-pad sample from the specimen in Stockholm (an earlier attempt by another team could not extract viable hoopoe starling DNA).

facts.statement: In 2024, Jérôme Fuchs and colleagues studied the Stockholm specimen and confirmed the hoopoe starling's close relations with the genera Sturnia, Leucopsar, and Sturnornis.
facts.quote: In 2024, French biologist Jérôme Fuchs and colleagues also studied the Stockholm sample, and confirmed the species' close relations with the starling genera Sturnia, Leucopsar, and Sturnornis.

facts.statement: The only known life drawing of the hoopoe starling was made by French artist Paul Philippe Sauguin de Jossigny in the early 1770s.
facts.quote: The only illustration of the hoopoe starling now thought to have been made from life was drawn by French artist Paul Philippe Sauguin de Jossigny during the early 1770s.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the hoopoe starling's population decline may have been caused by sea-level increases during the last interglacial period, which reduced its habitat on the island.
facts.quote: The decrease in its population was perhaps due to a sea-level increase caused by the last interglacial period, which reduced the bird's habitat on the island.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling was an omnivore that ate fruits, seeds, and insects.
facts.quote: Like most other starlings, the hoopoe starling was omnivorous, feeding on fruits, seeds, and insects.

facts.statement: The bird had a long, slender, sharp, and frayed tongue that may have moved rapidly to feed on fruit, nectar, pollen, and invertebrates.
facts.quote: Its tongue — long, slender, sharp, and frayed — may have been able to move rapidly, helpful when feeding on fruit, nectar, pollen, and invertebrates.

facts.statement: Robust pelvic elements and large feet and claws suggest the hoopoe starling foraged near the ground.
facts.quote: Its pelvic elements were robust and its feet and claws large, indicating that it foraged near the ground.

facts.statement: The bird had strong jaws and a skull similar to the hoopoe, likely used for probing and opening holes in the substrate.
facts.quote: Its jaws were strong; Morioka compared its skull to that of the hoopoe, and it may have foraged in a similar way, probing and opening holes in substrate by inserting and opening its beak.

facts.statement: Stomach contents of a dissected specimen included seeds and berries of Pseudobuxus, possibly Eugenia buxifolia.
facts.quote: De Montbeillard was informed of the stomach contents of a dissected specimen, consisting of seeds and the berries of "Pseudobuxus" (possibly Eugenia buxifolia, a bush with sweet, orange berries).

facts.statement: A specimen weighed 4 oz and was fatter during June and July.
facts.quote: He noted that the bird weighed 4 oz, and was fatter around June and July.

facts.statement: The hoopoe starling likely nested in tree cavities.
facts.quote: The hoopoe starling probably nested in tree cavities.

facts.statement: Research in 2020 noted the bird had black skin and light plumage, possibly an adaptation for protection against ultraviolet radiation.
facts.quote: Belgian biologist Michaël P. J. Nicolaï and colleagues pointed out in 2020 that the hoopoe starling had black skin combined with light plumage and lived in high irradiation zones, which may have evolved for protection against ultraviolet irradiation in this and other black-skinned birds.

facts.statement: Two specimens from Julien Desjardins' aviary were pickled and sent to the Paris museum in 1839.
facts.quote: Two specimens that had lived in the aviary of French natural historian Julien Desjardins were pickled and given to the Paris museum in 1839.

facts.statement: Captive birds could be fed bananas, potatoes, and chayote, while wild birds avoided inhabited areas.
facts.quote: Cordemoy recalled that captive birds could be fed a wide variety of food, such as bananas, potatoes, and chayote, and wild birds would never enter inhabited areas.

facts.statement: The last definite live specimen was taken in 1836.
facts.quote: The final specimen on the island (the last definite record of a live specimen anywhere) was taken in 1836.

facts.statement: There are 19 surviving specimens globally, including one skeleton and two in spirits, with two in Paris and four in Troyes.
facts.quote: There are 19 surviving hoopoe starling specimens in museums around the world (including one skeleton and two specimens preserved in spirits), with two in the Paris Museum and four in Troyes.

facts.statement: The only known subfossil specimen is a femur discovered in 1993 in a Réunion grotto.
facts.quote: The only known subfossil hoopoe starling specimen is a femur, discovered in 1993 in a Réunion grotto.

facts.statement: Specimens were sent to Europe starting in the late 18th century, with most collected in the early 19th century.
facts.quote: Specimens were sent to Europe beginning in the second half of the 18th century, with most collected during the first half of the 19th century.

facts.statement: Skins in Turin, Livorno, and Caen were destroyed in WWII, and four skins from Réunion and Mauritius have disappeared.
facts.quote: Additional skins in Turin, Livorno, and Caen were destroyed during World War II, and four skins have disappeared from Réunion and Mauritius (which now have one each).

facts.statement: It is unclear when specimens were acquired, and they were frequently moved between collections.
facts.quote: It is unclear when each specimen was acquired, and specimens were frequently moved between collections.

facts.statement: It is unclear which specimens served as the basis for descriptions and illustrations.
facts.quote: It is also unclear which specimens were the basis for which descriptions and illustrations.

facts.statement: It is often suggested that the introduction of the common myna caused competition between the two starling species.
facts.quote: An oft-repeated suggestion is that the introduction of the common myna (Acridotheres tristis) led to competition between these two starling species.

facts.statement: The common myna was introduced in 1759 to fight locusts but became a pest; the hoopoe starling coexisted with it for nearly 100 years, possibly without sharing habitat.
facts.quote: The myna was introduced to Réunion in 1759 to combat locusts, and became a pest itself, but the hoopoe starling coexisted with the myna for nearly 100 years and they may not have shared habitat.

facts.statement: Rats inhabited tree cavities and likely preyed on eggs, juveniles, and nesting birds.
facts.quote: Like the hoopoe starling, the rats inhabited tree cavities and would have preyed on eggs, juveniles, and nesting birds.

facts.statement: British ecologist Anthony S. Cheke identified predation by the wolf snake as the chief cause of extinction, noting the species survived other threats for generations.
facts.quote: According to British ecologist Anthony S. Cheke, this was the chief cause of the hoopoe starling's extinction; the species had survived for generations despite other threats.

facts.statement: Deforestation for plantations began in Réunion in the 1830s.
facts.quote: Beginning in the 1830s, Réunion was deforested for plantations.

facts.statement: After slavery was abolished in 1848, former slaves and white peasants cultivated pristine areas, pushing the hoopoe starling to the edges of its habitat.
facts.quote: Former slaves joined white peasants in cultivating pristine areas after slavery was abolished in 1848, and the hoopoe starling was pushed to the edges of its former habitat.

facts.statement: According to Hume, over-hunting by a growing population was the final blow to the species as forests became more accessible.
facts.quote: According to Hume, over-hunting was the final blow to the species; with forests more accessible, hunting by the rapidly growing human population may have driven the remaining birds to extinction.

facts.statement: Writers in the 1860s noted the bird had almost disappeared, likely already extinct, and Vinson in 1877 suggested the last individuals may have died in forest fires.
facts.quote: During the 1860s, various writers noted that the bird had almost disappeared, but it was probably already extinct by this time; in 1877, Vinson lamented that the last individuals might have been killed by recent forest fires.

facts.statement: Rodrigues and Mauritius starling species likely disappeared with rats, and rats contributed to the extinction of at least five Aplonis starling species in the Pacific.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues and Mauritius species probably disappeared with the arrival of rats; at least five species of Aplonis starlings have disappeared from the Pacific Islands, with rats also contributing to their extinction.
